stem: A bag contains 11 red marbles, 7 blue marbles, and 3 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is blue?
explanation: The total number of marbles is 11 + 7 + 3 = 21. The probability of selecting a blue marble is the number of blue marbles divided by the total: 7/21 (which simplifies to 1/3). The value 7/14 results from incorrectly using only the red and blue marbles as the total, ignoring the green marbles. The value 3/21 corresponds to selecting a green marble instead of blue. The value 11/21 corresponds to selecting a red marble instead of blue.

stem: In a class of 34 students, 19 play soccer, 13 play tennis, and 5 play both soccer and tennis. If a student is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student plays soccer or tennis?
explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle, the number of students who play soccer or tennis is 19 + 13 - 5 = 27. The probability is 27/34. The value 32/34 results from adding 19 + 13 without subtracting the 5 students who play both, double-counting them. The value 19/34 considers only soccer players, ignoring those who play tennis but not soccer. The value 22/34 results from an arithmetic error such as computing 19 + 13 - 5 as 22 instead of 27.

stem: A survey of 200 employees found the following: 74 work remotely, 126 work on-site, 41 of the remote workers have been with the company for more than 5 years, and 58 of the on-site workers have been with the company for more than 5 years. Given that a randomly selected employee has been with the company for more than 5 years, what is the probability that the employee works remotely?
explanation: The total number of employees with more than 5 years is 41 + 58 = 99. The conditional probability that an employee works remotely given they have more than 5 years is 41/99. The value 41/74 incorrectly uses the total number of remote workers as the denominator rather than the total number of employees with more than 5 years, confusing P(>5 years | remote) with P(remote | >5 years). The value 41/200 uses the entire employee population as the denominator, calculating the joint probability rather than the conditional probability. The value 58/99 gives the probability that a 5+ year employee works on-site, not remotely, reversing the numerator.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 250 voters in a city found that 62% support a new library bond. The margin of error for the survey is 4 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Between 58% and 66% of all voters in the city likely support the bond.
Exactly 62% of all voters in the city support the bond.
Between 62% and 66% of all voters in the city likely support the bond.
The survey is inaccurate because the margin of error is too large.

explanation: A margin of error of 4 percentage points means the true population proportion is plausibly within 4 points above or below the sample estimate: 62% - 4% = 58% to 62% + 4% = 66%. The statement that exactly 62% support the bond treats the sample statistic as the exact population parameter, ignoring sampling variability. The range 62% to 66% applies the margin of error in only one direction, omitting the lower bound. Claiming the survey is inaccurate because of the margin of error misunderstands the purpose of reporting a margin of error, which quantifies uncertainty rather than indicating a flaw.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 400 residents in a town and finds that 47% prefer expanded bus routes. A second random sample of 900 residents from the same town finds that 51% prefer expanded bus routes. Which of the following best explains why the second sample is more likely to produce a confidence interval that contains the true population proportion?

options.text: The larger sample size reduces the margin of error, producing a narrower and more precise interval.
The larger sample size guarantees the sample proportion equals the population proportion.
The larger sample eliminates all sampling bias.
The second sample's higher percentage is closer to 50%, making it more accurate.

explanation: Increasing the sample size decreases the standard error and thus the margin of error, yielding a narrower confidence interval that is more precise. A larger sample does not guarantee the sample proportion equals the population proportion; sampling variability always exists regardless of sample size. A larger sample reduces random sampling error but does not eliminate systematic bias, which is a design issue unrelated to sample size. The closeness of 51% to 50% is coincidental and does not inherently make an estimate more accurate; precision depends on sample size and sampling method, not the value of the estimate itself.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A polling organization surveys a random sample of 1,100 adults in a state and reports that 39% support a proposed tax change, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. A local newspaper claims that since 39% is less than 50%, the majority of adults in the state oppose the tax change. Which of the following is the most accurate critique of the newspaper's claim?

options.text: The confidence interval (36% to 42%) does not include 50%, so the claim that a majority opposes is supported by the data.
The claim is unjustified because some respondents may have no opinion, so those who oppose may not constitute a majority.
The claim is valid only if the sample was stratified by age and income.
The margin of error is too large to draw any conclusions about voter opinion.

explanation: The newspaper assumes that everyone who does not support the tax change opposes it. However, some respondents may be undecided or have no opinion, so 61% not supporting does not mean 61% actively oppose. Without knowing the breakdown between opposition and no opinion, the claim that a majority opposes is unjustified. The observation that the confidence interval (36% to 42%) excludes 50% confirms that fewer than half support the change, but this does not establish that a majority opposes it, since non-support includes undecided respondents. Requiring stratification by age and income conflates sampling methodology with the logical flaw in the claim. Saying the margin of error is too large to draw any conclusion is incorrect, as a 3-point margin of error at 95% confidence from 1,100 respondents is standard and adequate for inference.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A researcher wants to determine whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. She randomly assigns 60 tomato plants to two groups: one group receives the new fertilizer and the other receives no fertilizer. After 8 weeks, she measures the yield. What type of study is this?

options.text: An experiment, because a treatment is imposed on randomly assigned groups
An observational study, because the researcher measures an existing outcome
A survey, because data is collected from a sample of plants
An observational study, because no control group is used

explanation: Because the researcher randomly assigns plants to groups and imposes a treatment (fertilizer vs. no fertilizer), this is an experiment. Calling it an observational study because it measures an existing outcome ignores the key feature: the researcher actively manipulates the treatment variable rather than merely observing. Calling it a survey confuses data collection with study design; surveys collect self-reported data from people, which does not apply to plants receiving treatments. Claiming there is no control group is factually wrong, since the group receiving no fertilizer serves as the control.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A health agency observes that among 5,000 adults, those who drink green tea daily have lower rates of heart disease than those who do not. The agency concludes that drinking green tea reduces heart disease risk. Which of the following is the most significant flaw in the agency's conclusion?

options.text: The study is observational, so confounding variables may explain the association rather than a causal effect of green tea.
The sample size of 5,000 is too small to detect a meaningful difference.
The study did not measure how much green tea each person consumed per day.
The conclusion is valid because the agency used a large and diverse sample.

explanation: Because participants were not randomly assigned to drink or not drink green tea, this is an observational study. Confounding variables (such as overall diet, exercise habits, or socioeconomic status) may differ between the two groups and could explain the lower heart disease rate, making a causal claim unjustified. A sample of 5,000 is generally large enough for detecting meaningful health differences, so sample size is not the primary concern. While not measuring exact daily consumption is a limitation, it does not address the fundamental problem that correlation does not establish causation without random assignment. Claiming the conclusion is valid because of a large sample ignores the inability of observational studies to establish causation regardless of sample size.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers conduct a randomized controlled trial to test whether a new tutoring method improves standardized test scores. They recruit 300 volunteers from a single high school and randomly assign them to either the new tutoring method or traditional tutoring. After 12 weeks, students using the new method score an average of 37 points higher. Which of the following is a valid conclusion from this study?

options.text: The new tutoring method likely caused the higher scores among the participants, but the results may not generalize to students at other schools.
The new tutoring method causes higher scores for all high school students.
No causal conclusion can be drawn because the participants were volunteers.
The results prove that traditional tutoring is ineffective.

explanation: Random assignment of participants to treatment and control groups allows a causal inference: the new method likely caused the score improvement among these participants. However, since the sample consists of volunteers from a single school, the results cannot be generalized to all high school students. Claiming the method causes higher scores for all high school students overgeneralizes beyond the study population. While using volunteers does limit generalizability, the random assignment to groups within those volunteers still supports a causal conclusion about the treatment effect for the participants. Saying traditional tutoring is ineffective mischaracterizes the finding; a 37-point difference means the new method outperformed traditional tutoring, not that traditional tutoring produced no benefit.
